    AI Overview
    "Pinch" originated from Middle English (
    pinchen) and Anglo-French (pinchier), likely derived from a Vulgar Latin term for pricking, appearing around the 13th century. It generally refers to squeezing flesh between a thumb and finger, or using tools, and is used to describe tight clothing, small amounts of ingredients, or slang for stealing or arresting. 
    Common Uses and Contexts 
    • Physical Action: Squeezing skin or, in horticulture, removing buds/shoots to encourage growth.
    • Measurement: A tiny amount of powder, spice, or salt usually held between the thumb and forefinger, or, more specifically, a four-finger pinch for a quarter teaspoon.
    • Physical Distress:
      When shoes or clothes are too tight, causing uncomfortable pressure.
    • Economic Strain: "Pinching pennies" refers to extreme saving or being in a tight financial situation (e.g., "the pinch of the recession").
    • Slang: To steal or to be arrested (e.g., "he got pinched by the cops").
    • Technical: In music, a "pinch harmonic" is a guitar technique creating a high-pitched squeal. In climbing, an "Edelrid Pinch" is a specific type of belay device. 
    Why Pinching Hurts
    Pinching causes pain because it compresses skin, nerves, and blood vessels together, which triggers pain receptors (nociceptors) in the skin. It is sometimes used in medical contexts to test for dehydration (skin resiliency) or to measure body fat using skinfold calipers. 
    Types of Pinch 
    • Two-finger/Finger and Thumb: The standard grip.
    • Four-finger: Used for measurements.
    • Pinch Grip/Bar: A type of squeeze using tools, like a pinch bar for heavy objects. 
    Origin Details
    The earliest known use of the verb pinch is from around 1230. It likely shares roots with old terms for stinging or pointing, such as pungere (to prick) or pica (a spike).

    pinch
    /pin(t)SH/
    Learn to pronounce
    verb
    verb: pinch; 3rd person present: pinches; past tense: pinched; past participle: pinched; gerund or present participle: pinching
    1. 1.
      grip (something, typically someone's flesh) tightly and sharply between finger and thumb.
      "she pinched his cheek"
      h
      Similar:
      nip
      tweak
      squeeze
      compress
      grasp
      • use the fingers to remove (a bud or leaves) from a plant to encourage bushy growth.
        "pinch out tips of shoots regularly"
      • (of a shoe) hurt (a foot) by being too tight.
        "Mrs. Grandison's pointed, Italian-style shoes were already beginning to pinch her feet"
        h
        Similar:

        "Aunt Rose pinched her thin lips together"
    2. 2.

      "to explore in more detail just pinch the screen"

    Phrases
    in a pinch
    in a critical situation; if absolutely necessary.
    feel the pinch
    experience hardship, especially financial. "staff were beginning to feel the pinch as the dispute entered its third week"
    have to pinch oneself
    used to convey that a good situation is so surprising that the person involved has to make sure they are not imagining it. "sometimes I have to pinch myself to realize it isn't all a dream"
    Origin
    Middle English (as a verb): from an Old Northern French variant of Old French pincier ‘to pinch’.
